# Mineral fertiliser (guano, phosphate, potash, nitrate) (`mineral_fertiliser`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/agriculture.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Agriculture & food (`agriculture`)
- Deps: helped by sulphuric_acid, photosynthesis_plant_nutrition, ammonia_synthesis
- Core idea: Plants build their bodies from air and water but need a few mineral nutrients from the soil, above all nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium; the scarcest one limits the yield (law of the minimum). These can be supplied from outside the farm: nitrogen from seabird guano or Chilean nitrate, phosphorus from bones or rock phosphate made soluble with sulphuric acid (superphosphate, roughly equal weights of ground bone or rock and acid), potassium from wood ash or potash salts. Demonstration: plots with and without each nutrient, as at Rothamsted.
- Pitfalls:
  - Liebig's own error: he thought plants get enough nitrogen from the air and only minerals need replacing; cereals need added nitrogen
  - Overdosing: too much nitrogen makes cereals fall over (lodging) and scorches seedlings
  - Believing that humus is the food of plants (the old humus theory)
  - Using raw ground rock phosphate on neutral or limy soil; it is almost insoluble until treated with acid
  - Forgetting that guano and nitrate deposits are finite; Peru's guano was largely exhausted within forty years
- History: americas: pre-Columbian – coastal Peruvians and the Inca manure with seabird guano and protect the bird islands; 1830s Chilean nitrate exported; china: by Ming – bone ash, oil-seed cakes and lime sold as fertilisers; europe: 1804 Humboldt brings guano samples; 1828 Sprengel and 1840 Liebig state the mineral theory; 1842 Lawes patents superphosphate; 1843 Rothamsted experiments begin; 1840s guano boom; 1861 Stassfurt potash mined; 1913 synthetic ammonia
- Read:
  - Justus Liebig, Organic Chemistry in its Applications to Agriculture and Physiology (1840)
  - Gregory T. Cushman, Guano and the Opening of the Pacific World (2013)
  - Vaclav Smil, Enriching the Earth (2001)
